This change would probably eliminate most if not all of the benthic forms now present in the existing stream habitat, as well as the existing trout fishery.
7.3 SOCIO-ECONOMIC CONSIDERATIONS
The Applicant has estimated that approximately 100 new families of construction workers would relocate in the area surrounding the project. Some home developments could be expected in neighboring towns, such as Salem, South Carolina (8 miles from the project site), that could become permanent residences for these people as future construction projects are planned in the area.
Once the project is completed, the Applicant would make substantial contributions to the County of Oconee through taxes paid on the project lands and works. For the first 5 years, it is estimated that this would amount to $950,000 annually and thereafter $1,350,000 annually. This represents roughly 25 percent of Oconee's 1974 real and property tax revenues. The additional revenue could result in either increased government services to the local population or a lowering of the tax rate. In either case, the company's taxes would be an important revenue source for the county.
7.4 RESOURCES LOST
Resources that would be used in the construction and operation of the proposed project include land, minerals, supplies, water from Bad Creek, West Bad Creek, and Lake Jocassee, and human skill, labor, and capital. Most of the resource commitments such as the construction materials and supplies, would be irreversibly and irretrievably lost, except for those which could be salvaged after their use.
Approximately 820 acres of land would be used for the development of the proposed Bad Creek Project (Applicant's Exhibit W). About 505 acres of this total would be subsequently inundated or used for other project facilities, and therefore removed from use as wildlife habitat for the life of the project.
